title: Pasta all'Amatriciana
subtitle: tomato and guanciale pasta from Amatrice
excerpt: A bold, savoury tomato sauce built on cured pork and dried chilli. The fat from the bacon and the starch in the pasta water bind everything into a glossy coating. This is Roman trattoria cooking at its best.
sourceNotes: Amatriciana originates from the town of Amatrice in Lazio. It is one of the four cornerstone Roman pasta dishes and relies on guanciale (cured pork cheek).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce can be made up to 2 days ahead. Reheat gently and cook the pasta fresh.

content.text: Render the bacon slowly so the fat melts out. That fat becomes the base of the sauce. Do not drain it away.

items.prepNote: use guanciale or lardons -- cut into small cubes

content.text: Put the bacon in a cold dry frying pan. Set over medium-low heat. Let the fat render out slowly for 8 to 10 minutes until golden and slightly crisp. Do not rush this step.
Add the chilli flakes and stir for 30 seconds. If using wine, pour it in now and let it bubble until evaporated, about 2 minutes.
Add the crushed tomatoes. Season with pepper and a little salt (the bacon and cheese are both salty). Simmer for 15 minutes until reduced and rich.
Cook the pasta in a large pot of well-salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve a large mug of pasta water before draining.
Drain the pasta and add it to the sauce. Toss over medium heat, adding pasta water as needed. The sauce should coat each piece of pasta.
Remove from the heat. Add half the Pecorino and toss well. Serve in bowls with the remaining cheese on top.

items.cause: Too much fat left in the pan
items.fix: Spoon out some of the rendered fat before adding the tomatoes.
Simmer a few more minutes. Add more grated cheese and a splash of pasta water and toss vigorously.

content.text: Amatriciana comes from the mountain town of Amatrice, northeast of Rome. It became a Roman favourite over centuries. The dish is now protected by Italian law. Pecorino is the authentic cheese.
